common_name: Mostruosa di Sicilia Eggplant (Sicilian Monstrous Eggplant)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out only once nights stay reliably warm; this heirloom needs a long, hot season to size up its enormous fruit.

directions: Mostruosa di Sicilia is a traditional Sicilian eggplant grown for enormous, rounded fruit streaked white and lavender-purple that can reach several pounds apiece on a single sturdy plant. Give it fertile, well-drained soil, consistent moisture, and steady feeding to support the oversized fruit, and stake plants where wind or heavy fruit load threatens to topple them. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and the flesh firm, since oversized, dull-skinned fruit turns bitter and seedy; younger specimens are tender enough for grilling, stewing, or roasting whole in Sicilian caponata and parmigiana preparations. Because fruit size varies widely from seed, Sicilian gardeners traditionally let a few of the most impressive specimens mature fully for seed saving.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed; Pachino types thrive in lean, sandy, slightly saline soil and intense heat, so avoid overwatering or overly rich ground.

directions: Pachino takes its name from the town at Sicily's southeastern tip, where volcanic, sandy, mineral-rich soil and near-constant sun and sea breeze concentrate sugars in small, intensely flavored cherry and plum-shaped fruit, earning the tomato PGI (IGP) status in Italy. Grow on a trellis or stake and let the soil run drier than typical tomato culture, since mild water stress is part of what produces the variety's concentrated sweetness and thin, glossy skin. Fruit is traditionally harvested still on the vine in small clusters and sold or stored that way, since the cluster habit extends shelf life for weeks at room temperature. Use fresh in salads, on bruschetta, or simply halved and dressed with olive oil, where the tomato's natural sweetness needs little embellishment.
sources: Consorzio di Tutela Pomodoro di Pachino IGP

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring into lean, rocky, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; this volcanic-island strain is adapted to porous, mineral-rich ground and resents any standing moisture.

directions: This is the landrace selection grown for centuries on the volcanic island of Pantelleria off Sicily's southwest coast, where porous black lava soil, intense sun, and sea wind are credited with producing an unusually large, thick, aromatic flower bud now protected under Italian DOP status. Plants sprawl over dry stone terraces (the traditional 'conche' grown without irrigation), and buds are hand-picked daily at pea size before the flowers open, then cured for weeks in coarse sea salt and rinsed before use, developing a distinctively floral, pungent intensity more pronounced than brine-cured capers from other regions. Site it on a dry slope, raised bed, or rock wall where poor soil and reflected heat are an advantage, and resist the urge to fertilize or water beyond establishment. In the kitchen the cured buds season caponata, pasta alla Trapanese, swordfish involtini, and other signature western Sicilian dishes.

common_name: Spinoso di Palermo Artichoke (Palermo Spiny Artichoke)
scientific_name: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Spinoso di Palermo'

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or plant rooted offshoots in early spring; established clumps bloom through fall and winter in Sicily's mild Mediterranean climate.

directions: Grown in market gardens around Palermo and now protected as an IGP product, Spinoso di Palermo produces large, elongated, violet-green globes armed with long, sharp spines on the bracts, a trait many Sicilian cooks associate with superior flavor and tenderness in the heart compared to spineless modern hybrids. Handle harvested heads with gloves and a sharp knife, cutting the main terminal bud first to encourage a long season of smaller side buds through late winter. Rich, deep, well-drained soil and consistent moisture produce the best size, while mild Mediterranean-style winters without hard freezes let plants bloom nearly year-round. In the kitchen the tender hearts and bracts star in carciofi alla palermitana (stuffed and braised) and are prized sliced raw into salads while still young.
sources: Consorzio di Tutela Carciofo Spinoso di Palermo IGP

planting.note: Direct sow in late winter to early spring while soil is still cool; this small volcanic-island lentil is traditionally dry-farmed and grows best through a cool, rain-fed stretch before summer heat sets in.

directions: Grown on the small volcanic island of Ustica off Sicily's northern coast and recognized as a Slow Food Presidium, this lentil has been cultivated in tiny plots on mineral-rich volcanic soil for generations, surviving almost entirely on winter and spring rainfall with no irrigation. Plants are low, wiry, and bushy with small, pale, quick-cooking seeds that need no pre-soaking and hold a tender bite in soups and simple preparations dressed with local olive oil. Sow in lean soil without added nitrogen, since rich ground pushes foliage instead of pods, and hand-harvest or pull whole plants once most pods have dried and begun to rattle. The crop's isolation on a small island with no large-scale commercial lentil production has helped preserve a distinct, long-standing local landrace.

common_name: Fava Larga di Leonforte (Leonforte Broad Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow in autumn in mild Mediterranean climates for an overwintered crop, or as early as soil can be worked in colder zones; this Sicilian heirloom carries a long tradition of fall sowing around Leonforte in the Enna province.

directions: Named for the inland Sicilian town of Leonforte, this heirloom broad bean is prized for unusually large, flat pods that can hold six or more oversized, pale green seeds, a trait local growers have selected for over generations through careful seed saving. Direct sow an inch deep in cool, workable soil in fall or very early spring, spacing plants close so they lean on one another without staking in open ground. Harvest some pods young and tender to eat raw with young pecorino and a glass of wine in the classic Sicilian spring pairing, and let later pods mature and dry fully for storage as a dried pulse through the rest of the year. Pinch growing tips once the lowest pods have set to discourage aphids and push energy into filling the beans already underway.

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost in warm soil; this long-season Sicilian winter melon needs a full hot summer to fill out fruit that will then be stored and ripen further off the vine into winter.

directions: Purceddu is a traditional Sicilian landrace winter melon, smooth-skinned and pale green to yellow, grown across the island for its unusual keeping quality: fruit is harvested still under-ripe in late summer, then hung in nets or stored in a cool, dry place where it continues to slowly ripen and sweeten for weeks, traditionally lasting through the winter and often appearing on the Christmas table. Give vines full sun, rich soil, and even moisture through fruit set, then taper watering as fruit matures to improve storage quality. The pale flesh is milder and less aromatic than summer muskmelons, with a crisp texture that holds up well to the long storage period. Select only fully intact, unblemished fruit for storage, since any bruising or cracked skin shortens keeping time dramatically.

planting.note: Start seed indoors and transplant once nights stay warm, then withhold supplemental irrigation once plants establish; siccagno means 'dry-farmed' and the variety is traditionally grown on stored winter soil moisture alone.

directions: Pomodoro Siccagno, most famously grown in the Belice Valley of western Sicily and recognized as a Slow Food Presidium, is a rustic, irregularly shaped tomato traditionally raised without any irrigation beyond what deep winter rains leave stored in the clay-rich soil through the dry Sicilian summer. The resulting water stress concentrates sugars and acids into a smaller, thicker-skinned, deeply ribbed fruit with a flavor local growers describe as more intense than irrigated tomatoes, and the thick skin lets whole plants be pulled and hung indoors at season's end so fruit continues ripening for months. Space plants generously in deeply worked soil to encourage roots to range widely in search of residual moisture, and avoid the temptation to water once fruit set begins. Use fresh in salads, sun-dried, or cooked down into concentrated sauces that keep well into winter.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after frost danger passes; Interdonato is among the earliest-ripening lemons, with fruit ready from late summer into fall around its home region near Messina.

directions: Bred near Messina in 1875 by Colonel Giacomo Interdonato and believed to be a cross between lemon and citron, this is one of Sicily's oldest named citrus selections and is still grown commercially along the Ionian coast under IGP recognition. Trees produce elongated, thin-skinned, pale yellow fruit with relatively few seeds and a fine, aromatic rind that ripens unusually early, letting growers harvest ahead of other lemon cultivars and ahead of the first autumn storms. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, water deeply and regularly through fruit development, and protect from hard freezes, since it is less cold-hardy than Meyer lemon. The thin rind and pronounced aroma make it a favorite in Sicily for candying and for limoncello production, in addition to standard culinary juice and zest uses.
sources: Consorzio di Tutela Limone di Siracusa IGP
University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
